(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) — Watch out. Lock up your loved ones. Another bloated, overproduced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the laboratories of DreamWorks Animation, and it is poised to devour your children.

Susan, also known as “Ginormica,” must save the world in *Monsters vs. Aliens*. But there is no need for undue alarm: the film is relatively harmless—a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and only the barest excuse for a plot.

That may sound severe. After all, who would not want to watch a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles—the ultimate demolition roller derby? But consider that image for a moment. Roller skates work because their wheels are fixed. Try the same feat with motorcars, and you are unlikely to get very far.

Is that too fastidious a complaint? Perhaps. But Pixar would be unlikely to play quite so freely with the laws of physics, and that sort of inattention to detail is characteristic of the lackadaisical storytelling on display here, as in other DreamWorks animated features. Incidentally, the creative team for this film includes the directors of *Shrek 2* and *Shark Tale*, and the writers of *Kung Fu Panda* and *The Rocker*.

High concepts, top-tier voice talent, and scattershot pop-cultural references are no substitute for a coherent script.

The XXXL woman in question—dubbed “Ginormica” by her U.S. military guards—begins as the plain and petite Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon, until a meteorite strikes her just minutes before she is to marry the unctuous chauvinist Derek, voiced by Paul Rudd. Her sudden growth spurt spares her from that particular fate worse than death, even if, at first glance, her new companions do not appear to be much of an improvement.

They include Dr. Cockroach, voiced by Hugh Laurie, a mad scientist who semi-inadvertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B., voiced by Seth Rogen, an amorphous blue, jelly-like blob who gets along perfectly well without a brain; Missing Link, voiced by Will Arnett, a gung-ho amphibian who is all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus, who is not voiced by anyone because he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction fans may enjoy identifying the film’s many allusions to genre classics—*Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, *Invaders from Mars*, *The Fly*, *The Creature from the Black Lagoon*, *The Blob*, *Mothra*, and *Attack of the 50-Foot Woman*, for starters—and spotting a handful of clever touches. Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, for instance, riffs on George C. Scott in *Dr. Strangelove*.

The problem is that, once the introductions are complete, the filmmakers have little to offer beyond a desperately limp plot. The White House enlists these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from the villainous Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson: a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, assisted by a one-eyed tin robot that does his dirty work.

Ginormica receives a kick-butt finale and emerges as a far stronger character—in several senses—than the movie’s president. In a genuinely witty piece of casting, the president is voiced by Stephen Colbert. That may be good politics, or at least a shrewd marketing decision from the studio’s perspective; it has been some time since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character, unless one counts *Coraline*, which was far too frightening for my family. Still, Susan’s self-esteem takes an awfully long time to arrive.

iReport.com: What do you think of *Monsters vs. Aliens*?

Bizarrely—and perhaps it is only my imagination—Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder: would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

Visually, too, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is undistinguished, though its shortcomings may be less apparent if viewed in 3-D. It is curious how often 3-D films produce two-dimensional characters, with *Coraline* again standing as the exception to the rule.

Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, *Monsters vs. Aliens* ought to be a great deal of fun—and, in places, it is. But the truth is that the film is as self-absorbed as Susan’s preening fiancé. Hand on heart, I had a better time at *Space Chimps*.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For *Entertainment Weekly*’s take, click here.

(CNN) — Brace yourself. Hide the family. Yet another oversized, heavily manufactured, big-idea creature feature has lumbered out of DreamWorks Animation and is headed straight for the children.

In “Monsters vs. Aliens,” Susan — later renamed “Ginormica” — is tasked with rescuing the planet. Still, there is no great reason to panic. The movie is mostly innocuous: a mild, fangless spoof with an automatic feminist angle and only the barest outline of a story.

That may sound severe. After all, who would not be tempted by the image of a 50-foot-tall woman tearing through San Francisco on “skates” that are actually cars — basically the most destructive roller derby imaginable? But pause on that idea for a moment. Roller skates function because their wheels stay fixed in place. Substitute automobiles and the concept falls apart pretty quickly.

Is that nitpicking? Maybe. But Pixar would be unlikely to treat basic physics with such casual disregard, and that looseness is typical of the careless approach to story found here and in other DreamWorks animated movies. For the record, this film’s creative roster includes directors from “Shrek 2” and “Shark Tale,” along with writers from “Kung Fu Panda” and “The Rocker.”

A flashy premise, famous voice actors and random pop-culture nods cannot make up for the absence of a solid screenplay.

The extra-extra-extra-large woman at the center of the film, called “Ginormica” by her U.S. military keepers, begins as ordinary, small-framed Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon. Just minutes before she is due to marry the oily, sexist Derek, voiced by Paul Rudd, she is struck by a meteorite. The impact causes her to grow enormously, sparing her from that particular fate worse than death — though her new companions do not initially seem like much of an upgrade.

They include Dr. Cockroach, voiced by Hugh Laurie, a deranged scientist who more or less accidentally fused himself with an insect; B.O.B., voiced by Seth Rogen, a shapeless blue gelatinous mass who manages perfectly well without a brain; Missing Link, voiced by Will Arnett, an aggressive amphibian with plenty of attitude; and Insectosaurus, a gigantic dust mite who has no voice actor because he has no dialogue.

Science-fiction buffs may enjoy ticking off the many allusions to older genre staples, including “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Invaders from Mars,” “The Fly,” “The Creature from the Black Lagoon,” “The Blob,” “Mothra” and “Attack of the 50-Foot Woman,” among others. There are also a few genuinely sharp touches, such as Kiefer Sutherland’s General W.R. Monger, who plays off George C. Scott’s performance in “Dr. Strangelove.”

The problem comes after the characters have been introduced. At that point, the filmmakers can only set in motion a painfully weak plot: the White House calls on these monster-heroes to defend Earth from the villainous Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson. Gallaxhar is a squid-like alien with four eyes, eight legs and a one-eyed metal robot carrying out his orders.

Ginormica does get a forceful action climax, and she is a far stronger figure — in more than one sense — than the film’s president, who is amusingly voiced by Stephen Colbert. From the studio’s point of view, that may be smart politics, or at least smart marketing. It has been some time since a family animated film offered a truly strong female character, unless one counts “Coraline,” which was far too frightening for my household. Even so, Susan takes an awfully long time to arrive at self-confidence.

iReport.com asks: What do you think of “Monsters vs. Aliens”?

Oddly — and perhaps this is only in my head — Gallaxhar has a slight resemblance to President Obama. Which raises the question: would that make Susan/Ginormica a stand-in for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

On the visual side, “Monsters vs. Aliens” is not especially memorable either, though some of its weaknesses may be less obvious in the 3-D version. It is curious how often 3-D films produce flat characters, with “Coraline” once again standing as the exception.

Loose, jokey and cheerfully junky, “Monsters vs. Aliens” ought to be a good time — and now and then, it is. But ultimately, the movie is as self-absorbed as Susan’s vain fiancé. Honestly, I enjoyed “Space Chimps” more.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” is 94 minutes long and rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly’s review, click here.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” comes across as a typically over-produced DreamWorks animated feature: loud, colorful, crowded with jokes, and determined to appeal to both children and adults at once. The film begins with a promising high-concept premise, combining 1950s monster-movie parody with modern blockbuster spectacle. Susan, an ordinary woman who is struck by a meteor on her wedding day, grows to enormous size and is renamed Ginormica by the government. She is locked away with a group of other strange creatures, only to become humanity’s best hope when Earth is threatened by an alien invasion.

The movie clearly wants to be more than a simple children’s adventure. It plays with familiar monster-film references, throws in pop-culture gags, and gives Susan a mild feminist arc in which she learns not to define herself by her shallow fiancé or by society’s expectations. In theory, this story of a woman literally outgrowing the life planned for her could have had real comic and emotional force. Susan’s transformation into Ginormica gives the film its strongest idea: she becomes powerful only after being treated as a freak, and she eventually discovers that independence is better than returning to her old, limited existence.

However, the critic finds that the film does very little with its best material. Instead of developing its characters or sharpening its satire, “Monsters vs. Aliens” relies on noise, speed, celebrity voices, and a steady stream of references. The supporting monsters are designed more as comic concepts than as fully realized personalities, and many of the jokes feel tossed in rather than carefully built. The movie seems eager to remind viewers of other films, genres, and bits of popular culture, but it rarely turns those references into anything especially clever or memorable.

Compared with Pixar’s work, the film feels careless. Pixar films are often praised for strong storytelling, emotional structure, and attention to character; by contrast, this DreamWorks production appears to assume that a clever premise and flashy execution are enough. The animation may be polished, the action may be energetic, and the voice cast may be famous, but those elements cannot disguise the weakness of the writing. The result is not a disaster, and it is not especially offensive. It is mostly harmless entertainment, with enough bright images and broad humor to keep younger audiences occupied.

Still, the critic’s overall judgment is that “Monsters vs. Aliens” is a missed opportunity. It has the ingredients for a smart parody and a satisfying empowerment story, but it never fully commits to either. Instead, it becomes another busy studio product: amusing in places, visually extravagant, and instantly forgettable. Its monsters, aliens, and celebrity performers may attract attention, but they cannot compensate for a story that feels underwritten and emotionally thin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style movie review of DreamWorks Animation’s “Monsters vs. Aliens,” summarizing the plot, voice cast, sci-fi references, 3-D visuals, and giving a mostly negative critical assessment.
counterfactuals.output:
DreamWorks Animation’s **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** arrives with a high-concept title, a flashy 3-D presentation and a deep bench of comic voice talent — but the result is more noisy product than inspired parody.

The film follows **Susan Murphy** (**Reese Witherspoon**), a California bride-to-be who is struck by a meteor on her wedding day and suddenly grows to nearly 50 feet tall. Renamed **Ginormica** by the government, she is shipped to a secret facility where the military has been storing other oddities: the gelatinous **B.O.B.** (**Seth Rogen**), the mad-scientist-insect hybrid **Dr. Cockroach** (**Hugh Laurie**), the gill-man **The Missing Link** (**Will Arnett**) and the towering bug **Insectosaurus**.

Their chance at freedom comes when Earth is threatened by the alien villain **Gallaxhar** (**Rainn Wilson**), prompting General W.R. Monger (**Kiefer Sutherland**) to unleash the monsters as humanity’s last line of defense. **Stephen Colbert** also turns up as a preening U.S. president, in one of the movie’s more openly satirical touches.

The movie is packed with affectionate references to classic sci-fi and monster cinema: **“Attack of the 50 Foot Woman,” “The Blob,” “The Fly,” “Creature from the Black Lagoon,” “Mothra,” “Godzilla”** and assorted 1950s alien-invasion pictures. The premise clearly wants to function as both homage and sendup, mixing retro B-movie imagery with modern computer-animation spectacle.

Visually, **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** is slick, colorful and designed to show off its then-prominent **3-D** format. There are meteors, missiles, giant robots, exploding spacecraft and plenty of shots staged to poke out of the screen. Some of the action sequences have scale and polish, and younger viewers may respond to the simple monster-team dynamic.

But the film’s weaknesses are hard to miss. For all its references, the satire is thin and the jokes are hit-or-miss, often leaning on one-note character gags rather than genuinely sharp writing. The voice cast is talented, but several performers seem trapped inside broadly sketched roles. Witherspoon gives Susan some warmth, yet the character’s empowerment arc feels mechanical. Rogen’s B.O.B. gets laughs, but the routine wears down. Wilson’s villain is more concept than character.

The biggest problem is that **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** feels engineered more than imagined. It has the ingredients of a clever animated sci-fi comedy — monsters, aliens, government absurdity, retro movie nostalgia — but rarely finds a fresh angle on them. The 3-D visuals provide momentary pop, yet they can’t disguise a story that is predictable, overbusy and surprisingly bland.

As family entertainment, it is watchable. As a DreamWorks showcase, it is technically competent. But as a comedy or a loving monster-movie spoof, **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** is mostly a missed opportunity: loud, polished and curiously forgettable.

**Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” is big, bright — and strangely small where it counts**

DreamWorks Animation’s *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives with the subtlety of a UFO crashing into a wedding, which is to say: not much. It is loud, glossy, eager to please, and packed with enough retro sci-fi references to keep parents mildly amused while children soak up the spectacle. What it is not, unfortunately, is especially well told.

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan Murphy, a bride-to-be who is struck by a meteorite and promptly grows into the towering Ginormica — a name that sounds less like a superhero identity than a rejected toy-line pitch. Hauled away by the government, she is grouped with other imprisoned oddities and eventually recruited to fight an alien invasion. It’s a promising setup: a woman literally outgrows the life everyone expected her to have. But the movie treats that idea with the depth of a bumper sticker.

Witherspoon brings warmth and comic timing to Ginormica, and the character’s arc — from anxious fiancée to self-possessed hero — is easily the film’s strongest emotional thread. The problem is that the screenplay keeps mistaking movement for momentum. Things crash, lasers fire, monsters banter, and yet the story rarely feels like it’s building toward anything more meaningful than the next set piece.

The supporting creatures are amusing in bursts, especially the gelatinous B.O.B., but they often feel like a committee’s idea of “quirky.” The jokes land just often enough to keep the film airborne, though not gracefully. For every clever gag, there’s another that seems engineered by spreadsheet.

And then there’s the inevitable comparison: Pixar. Fair or not, any major animated feature with big emotions and bigger visuals gets measured against the studio that turned toys, fish, robots and old men into existential poetry. By that standard, *Monsters vs. Aliens* comes up short. Pixar’s best films tend to smuggle emotional sophistication into family entertainment. DreamWorks, here, mostly smuggles in noise.

Visually, the movie has energy, color and scale, particularly in its monster-movie homage moments. But spectacle can only do so much heavy lifting. Beneath the polished animation and celebrity voices is a story that feels undercooked — a collection of concepts in search of a spine.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is not a disaster. It’s too cheerful, too fast and too intermittently funny for that. But for a movie about gigantic transformations, it remains disappointingly lightweight. Ginormica may be 49 feet tall, but the storytelling rarely rises above average.

## Review: *Monsters vs. Aliens* — Big Creatures, Bigger Noise, Modest Payoff

DreamWorks Animation’s 2009 film *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives with a premise that sounds delightfully absurd: classic creature-feature monsters are recruited by the U.S. government to defend Earth from an extraterrestrial threat. It has the ingredients for sharp satire, broad comedy, and retro sci-fi fun. Unfortunately, while the film is colorful and energetic, it often feels more like a collection of noisy set pieces than a fully satisfying animated adventure.

The story centers on Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon, whose wedding day is derailed when she is struck by a meteorite and grows to gigantic proportions. Renamed “Ginormica” by the government, she is taken to a secret facility where other monsters have been hidden away for years. There she meets the gelatinous and cheerful B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), the mad-scientist hybrid Dr. Cockroach Ph.D. (Hugh Laurie), the fish-ape Missing Link (Will Arnett), and the massive grub-like Insectosaurus.

This ensemble should be the film’s greatest strength, and occasionally it is. Rogen’s B.O.B. gets some of the best laughs, largely because his cluelessness is played with commitment. Laurie brings a dry wit to Dr. Cockroach, while Arnett’s Missing Link offers a fun, if underused, parody of macho monster-movie heroes. Witherspoon gives Susan a likable sense of frustration and self-discovery, though the script’s empowerment arc is fairly predictable.

The alien threat comes in the form of Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson, a villain with grand ambitions but limited comic impact. He is loud, theatrical, and designed to be ridiculous, but the writing rarely gives him enough bite to become memorable. Kiefer Sutherland also appears as General W.R. Monger, a military figure whose over-the-top authority adds to the film’s parody of Cold War-era monster movies and government secrecy.

Visually, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is bright and slick, with several action sequences clearly built to take advantage of the film’s original 3D release. The problem is that the spectacle often overwhelms the story. Jokes come quickly, but not all of them land, and the movie sometimes mistakes frantic movement for comic timing. Its affection for old sci-fi and monster films is obvious, but the satire remains fairly shallow, aiming more for easy gags than clever reinvention.

Still, the film has enough charm to keep younger viewers entertained, and its message about Susan finding confidence beyond her former life gives it a bit of emotional grounding. For adults, however, *Monsters vs. Aliens* may feel like a missed opportunity: a clever concept softened into a safe, marketable animated comedy.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* runs 94 minutes and is rated PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor, and mild language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a full-length negative review of DreamWorks’ “Monsters vs. Aliens” in the style of a newspaper or CNN entertainment critic, focusing on its overproduced concept, feminist theme, pop-culture references, and lack of coherent plot.
counterfactuals.output:
**Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” Is Big, Loud, and Strangely Hollow**

DreamWorks Animation’s *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives with all the polish, noise, and marketing muscle of a studio convinced that more is more: more characters, more references, more celebrity voices, more explosions, more 3-D spectacle. What it lacks is the one thing that might have made any of that matter — a coherent reason to exist beyond the pitch meeting.

The film begins with Susan Murphy, a mild-mannered bride-to-be, being struck by a mysterious meteorite on her wedding day. The impact transforms her into a towering, white-haired giantess, promptly renamed Ginormica by the government and locked away with a collection of other “monsters”: a brilliant cockroach scientist, a missing-link fish-man, a gelatinous blob, and an enormous grub-like creature. When aliens attack Earth, the government decides these imprisoned oddities are humanity’s best chance at survival.

On paper, that premise has potential. It sounds like a loving parody of 1950s monster movies and Cold War science-fiction paranoia, with room for satire, character comedy, and visual imagination. But *Monsters vs. Aliens* doesn’t develop the concept so much as inflate it. The film is so busy announcing its bigness that it rarely pauses to build stakes, relationships, or even jokes that feel earned. It is a movie built like a parade float: colorful, oversized, carefully engineered — and emotionally weightless.

The central arc is clearly meant to be empowering. Susan begins as a woman who has defined herself through her relationship with a self-absorbed fiancé, then gradually realizes she does not need to shrink herself — literally or figuratively — for anyone. The feminist theme is not subtle, and there is nothing wrong with that. Children’s films can and should handle big ideas directly. The problem is that the movie treats empowerment less as a lived transformation than as a branding exercise.

Susan’s journey is framed as a liberation from a shallow man and a small life, but the film gives her so little inner complexity that her awakening feels prepackaged. She is “empowered” because the screenplay says she is, because the action climax requires it, and because the movie wants applause for having a heroine who grows tall instead of waiting to be rescued. It is a worthwhile message delivered with the nuance of a billboard. The film gestures toward female self-realization, but too often it confuses height with depth.

The supporting monsters fare even worse. Each seems designed around a single gag: the mad scientist cockroach, the dim blob, the macho fish-man. Their personalities are loud but thin, and their interactions rarely evolve beyond cartoonish banter. DreamWorks has often specialized in the rapid-fire, reference-heavy animated comedy, and *Monsters vs. Aliens* may be one of the clearest examples of that formula running on autopilot. The movie tosses out pop-culture nods, genre references, and throwaway lines with the anxious energy of someone afraid the audience might stop looking at the screen for two seconds.

There are winks at old monster movies, sci-fi staples, government paranoia, superhero teams, disaster films, and celebrity culture. Some land mildly. Most simply evaporate. The references rarely sharpen the satire or deepen the world; they function as recognition buttons. Adults may notice the allusions, children may enjoy the slapstick, but the film never fuses those layers into something clever or memorable. It does not parody classic science fiction so much as raid its closet.

The alien villain, Gallaxhar, is similarly undercooked. He is introduced as a galactic menace, but he never becomes more than a generic animated antagonist with a booming voice and a vague plan. His motivations are barely sketched, his menace is inconsistent, and his presence mainly serves to push the film from one set piece to the next. That would be forgivable if the set pieces had comic momentum or visual surprise, but too many of them feel assembled rather than directed — scenes designed to showcase scale, not story.

The plot, such as it is, proceeds in chunks: Susan transforms, Susan is captured, the monsters are introduced, an alien robot attacks, the team is deployed, Susan learns confidence, the villain escalates, the finale arrives. There is a mechanical clarity to that structure, but little narrative flow. The film keeps changing shape without ever gathering force. Characters make decisions because it is time for the next sequence, not because the story has made those decisions inevitable.

This is especially frustrating because the film is not without assets. The animation is bright and technically accomplished. There are scattered jokes that work, particularly in the margins. The voice cast is energetic, and the retro sci-fi aesthetic occasionally gives the film a fun, pulpy texture. But those strengths are overwhelmed by the sense of a movie trying to be everything at once: a feminist coming-of-age story, a monster spoof, an alien-invasion comedy, a superhero team origin story, a 3-D thrill ride, and a celebrity-driven family product.

The result is overproduced in the most familiar modern animated way. Every surface gleams, every action beat is polished, every comic side character is calibrated for maximum trailer appeal. Yet the film feels impersonal. It has been focus-grouped into constant motion but not shaped into a satisfying story. It is less a movie than a bundle of marketable elements orbiting a theme.

For younger children, *Monsters vs. Aliens* may provide enough color, chaos, and broad humor to pass the time. But as family entertainment, it falls short of the best animated films, which understand that imagination is not the same as clutter and that a message is not the same as a character arc. Its heroine grows to enormous size, but the movie around her remains surprisingly small.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* wants to celebrate the strange, the powerful, and the underestimated. Too bad it does so in a film that feels less like a bold act of imagination than a studio committee’s idea of one.

**Movie Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” is big, bright — and surprisingly hollow**

DreamWorks Animation’s **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** arrives with a supersized premise, a marquee voice cast and the added promise of 3-D spectacle. But despite its colorful mayhem and occasional laughs, the film feels more like a loud demo reel than a fully satisfying animated feature.

The story follows **Susan Murphy** (voiced by **Reese Witherspoon**), a bride-to-be who is struck by a meteor and transformed into the 49-foot-11-inch giantess Ginormica. She is whisked away to a secret government facility, where she meets a collection of imprisoned “monsters”: the gelatinous **B.O.B.** (**Seth Rogen**), brilliant cockroach scientist **Dr. Cockroach** (**Hugh Laurie**), macho fish-ape hybrid **The Missing Link** (**Will Arnett**) and massive grub-like **Insectosaurus**. When alien invader **Gallaxhar** (**Rainn Wilson**) threatens Earth, General W.R. Monger (**Kiefer Sutherland**) enlists the monsters to fight back, while the film throws in comic turns from **Stephen Colbert** as the president and **Paul Rudd** as Susan’s self-absorbed fiancé.

Visually, the movie is polished in the reliable DreamWorks way: slick surfaces, exaggerated designs and action sequences engineered for maximum motion. But the animation rarely achieves the warmth, subtlety or emotional texture associated with Pixar’s best work. Where Pixar tends to build entire worlds that feel lived-in, “Monsters vs. Aliens” often feels like a parade of concepts — a giant woman, a blob, a mad scientist, a bug monster — without enough imagination beneath the designs.

The humor is similarly hit-or-miss. Rogen’s B.O.B. gets some of the better throwaway lines, and Colbert’s president supplies a few amusing moments of absurdity. Still, the comedy leans heavily on one-note gags, pop-culture winks and volume. The film wants to be both a retro sci-fi spoof and a kid-friendly action comedy, but too many jokes feel manufactured rather than inspired.

Character development is the biggest weakness. Susan’s journey from overlooked fiancée to empowered hero should give the film its heart, but the emotional beats are broad and predictable. Witherspoon brings likability to the role, yet Susan’s transformation is more scripted than deeply felt. The supporting monsters are fun in outline, but they remain largely defined by their gimmicks. Compared with Pixar characters, who often reveal surprising layers over the course of a story, this crew rarely gets beyond the punchline stage.

The much-promoted **3-D** is also a mixed blessing. “Monsters vs. Aliens” clearly builds scenes around the format, with objects flying toward the viewer and action staged for depth. But the effect often calls attention to itself instead of enhancing the story. After the initial novelty wears off, the 3-D feels less like a cinematic breakthrough than a theme-park attraction stretched to feature length.

The comparison is especially unflattering coming soon after **“Coraline,”** a darker, stranger and far more visually distinctive 3-D animated film. “Coraline” used depth to create mood and unease; “Monsters vs. Aliens” uses it mostly to poke the audience in the eye. And against Pixar’s standard of storytelling sophistication, DreamWorks’ film comes off as energetic but shallow.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” is not without charm. Younger viewers may enjoy its slapstick, bright colors and monster-team antics. But for an animated adventure with such a big cast and bigger scale, it ultimately feels small where it counts: imagination, emotion and lasting impact.
